passage: When I look back, the first year was mostly quiet waiting. Sarika and I had been friends since college, and when I finally brought her home for my cousin's engagement, my aunt asked, "Which family is she from?" and her face changed when I answered. Sarika's caste was different from ours. Later my aunt spoke about "our own people", and my mother wouldn't look at me. I wanted to shout. Instead I told them the truth at the dinner table: Sarika was the person who sat with me through the worst weeks of my father's illness. I didn't demand that they approve. I kept inviting Sarika, and I kept standing beside her when the aunts went quiet. After eight months my aunt sent her a plate of pedas. It wasn't an apology. It was a beginning. Sudha

qa.q: How long did it take before Sudha's aunt sent Sarika a plate of pedas?
qa.a: After eight months Sudha's aunt sent Sarika a plate of pedas.

qa.q: What did Sudha feel at the start, and what did Sudha do with that feeling?
qa.a: Sudha felt angry and hurt and wanted to shout, but chose to tell the truth calmly at the dinner table instead.

qa.q: Which choice by Sudha mattered more than winning the argument in one go?
qa.a: Sudha did not demand approval. Sudha kept inviting Sarika and stood beside her when the aunts went quiet, so trust could grow slowly.

qa.q: How might Sarika have felt when the aunts went quiet, and what did Sudha's presence mean?
qa.a: Probably uncomfortable and anxious. Sudha standing beside her showed that she was not facing the silence alone.

grounding: A young adult forms a close bond with a friend across caste and faces relatives' worry, responding with patience, honesty and loyalty.

subtopic: Caste and class awareness, discrimination recognition and fair conduct
passage: Note from the community counsellor, Tuesday. Raghav, 24, came in worried. He has been seeing Jomol for a year, and she belongs to a different caste from his family. His uncle shouted when he heard, and Raghav's first idea was to leave home that night. I asked him to wait a week. We talked about what his uncle fears (gossip, and losing face with relatives) and what Raghav actually wants to say. On Saturday Raghav told his mother calmly that Jomol matters to him and that he will not lie about it, and asked whether she would meet Jomol once. His mother said she needed time. I have booked a follow-up for the fortnight, and I suggested he keep asking, not push.

qa.q: How long has Raghav been seeing Jomol?
qa.a: Raghav has been seeing Jomol for a year.

qa.q: What is Raghav feeling when he thinks of leaving home that night?
qa.a: Raghav feels hurt, afraid and angry after his uncle shouted, and wants to escape the conflict.

qa.q: Which choice by Raghav on Saturday kept the door open?
qa.a: He told his mother calmly that Jomol matters to him and that he will not lie, and asked her to meet Jomol once instead of leaving.

qa.q: What might Raghav's uncle be afraid of?
qa.a: Gossip and losing face with relatives, which the counsellor noted as the uncle's fears. Anger may be covering that worry.

grounding: A young adult in love across caste faces an uncle's anger and chooses honesty and patience with family over an ultimatum.

passage: At nursery circle time, Anjali, five, kept staring at the small orange cloth tied over Gurnoor's hair. "Why is your hair wrapped?" she asked at last. "It's a patka," said Gurnoor. "My family wears it." Anjali turned to Mr. Bhupen, the teacher. "Sir, why?" He smiled. "Gurnoor's family has its own way of praying and dressing, and yours has its own." Anjali thought. "Can I see it?" Gurnoor nodded and let her touch the soft cloth. "We light a diya at home," said Anjali. "That's lovely," said Mr. Bhupen. She went back to her blocks with Gurnoor beside her.

qa.q: What was Gurnoor wearing over his hair?
qa.a: Gurnoor was wearing a small orange cloth called a patka.

qa.q: What is Anjali feeling as she stares and asks her questions?
qa.a: Anjali is curious. She wants to understand and is not afraid, so she asks straight out and then asks to see it.

qa.q: What choice did Mr. Bhupen make in answering, and what followed?
qa.a: He gave a simple, honest answer that each family has its own way of praying and dressing. Anjali stayed curious and shared that her family lights a diya.

qa.q: How might Gurnoor have felt when Anjali touched the cloth?
qa.a: Probably comfortable and proud, since he nodded and let her touch it, and then played beside her.

grounding: A child notices a friend who dresses and prays differently and asks why, and a simple honest answer keeps the curiosity open.

passage: I live opposite Madhav's flat and saw it from the lift lobby on Eid morning. Mohit, five, stared at the small embroidered cap on his friend Imran's head. "Why do you have a hat today?" Imran's father said, "We are going to the mosque to pray, and this is what some of us wear. Today is Eid, our special day." Mohit's eyes went wide. "Happy Eid!" he shouted. Madhav laughed, "Eid Mubarak, bhai." I can't say what Mohit was thinking, but he hopped on one foot all the way home, asking if he could borrow a cap for a game.

qa.q: What was Imran wearing on Eid morning?
qa.a: Imran was wearing a small embroidered cap.

qa.q: What might Mohit be feeling when he asks about the hat and then shouts "Happy Eid!"?
qa.a: Mohit seems curious and excited, with wide eyes and hopping. The neighbour cannot be sure what he thinks inside.

qa.q: Which choice by Imran's father kept Mohit's curiosity open?
qa.a: He answered simply and truthfully, saying they were going to the mosque to pray and it was their special day, Eid.

qa.q: How might Imran have felt when Mohit shouted "Happy Eid!"?
qa.a: Probably pleased and proud, since the greeting was warm and curious, not mocking.

grounding: A child notices a friend's different clothes and asks why, and a simple honest answer keeps curiosity open and free of fear.

passage: When I was nine, my mother let me carry a steel plate of Diwali laddoos to the neighbours. My favourite door was Seema Aunty's. She always said, "Wait, wait, don't go," and came back with a small bowl of something. That evening it was kheer. In the summer she had sent sewaiyan to us for Eid, and I had carried back a bowl of our sweet rice. I remember walking home slowly with the warm bowl, thinking that food goes both ways on our floor. That night I could smell sugar and cardamom from three different kitchens. It felt as if the whole building was having one big party. Jagdish

qa.q: What did Seema Aunty give Jagdish that evening?
qa.a: Seema Aunty gave Jagdish a small bowl of kheer.

qa.q: How did Jagdish feel walking home with the warm bowl?
qa.a: Jagdish felt happy and connected, as if the whole building was having one big party. 😊

qa.q: Which small gesture made the festival feel bigger than one home?
qa.a: Carrying sweets to the neighbours and getting bowls back, so that food went both ways on their floor.

qa.q: How might Seema Aunty have felt when Jagdish arrived with laddoos?
qa.a: Glad and warm. She said "Wait, wait, don't go" and came back with a bowl to share, which shows she enjoyed the exchange.

grounding: A child shares festival food with neighbours and feels part of something bigger than one home.

passage: Note to parents, Class 4, after the Eid weekend. Tanvir, 9, arrived on Monday with a tiffin of sewaiyan and a paper bag of small bowls. He said, "Ammi made lots so I can give one to everybody." He went round the class and gave each child a bowl, including Joseph and Kavya, who had shared their Christmas and Diwali sweets with him earlier. He gave the last bowl to the school guard, who smiled and said, "Eid Mubarak, beta." Tanvir looked proud all morning. I asked why he shared so much. He said, "Because then everyone is in Eid." I have thanked his mother and will invite all children to describe a festival at home next week. Ramesh, class teacher 🙂

qa.q: What did Tanvir bring to school on Monday?
qa.a: Tanvir brought a tiffin of sewaiyan and a paper bag of small bowls.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling as he gave out the bowls?
qa.a: Tanvir was proud and happy, wanting everyone to be part of Eid, as he said: "Then everyone is in Eid."

qa.q: What choice did Ramesh make after seeing Tanvir share?
qa.a: Ramesh thanked Tanvir's mother and planned to invite all the children to describe a festival at home, so the sharing could continue.

qa.q: How might the school guard have felt receiving the last bowl?
qa.a: Pleased and included, since the guard smiled and said "Eid Mubarak, beta."

grounding: A child shares Eid sweets with classmates and others and feels part of something bigger than one home.

passage: The school trip bus had a puncture, and the lunch stop shrank to twenty minutes. Rukmini, fifteen, opened her steel tiffin under a tree. A boy from the back row grinned. "Jains can't eat after dark, right? Is your family scared of ghosts?" A few laughed. Rukmini's face went hot and she closed the lid halfway. "It's not a joke," she said, but her voice came out small. Vandana, sitting beside her, said clearly, "That's her family's belief, and it's not funny. Would you laugh at your grandmother's fast?" The boy shrugged. Ms. Narang, the teacher, had overheard. When the bus started, she stood at the front. "Making fun of what a family believes is not humour. The ghost idea is simply wrong. Rukmini, I'm sorry that happened." Rukmini nodded and finally took a bite.

qa.q: What did the boy from the back row ask Rukmini?
qa.a: The boy asked whether Jains can't eat after dark and whether Rukmini's family is scared of ghosts.

qa.q: How does Rukmini feel when the boy jokes, and what shows it?
qa.a: Rukmini feels hurt and ashamed. Her face goes hot, she closes the lid halfway and her voice comes out small.

qa.q: Which choice by Ms. Narang helped protect Rukmini?
qa.a: Ms. Narang spoke to everyone on the bus, said that mocking a family's belief is not humour, named the ghost idea as wrong, and apologised to Rukmini.

qa.q: How might Vandana see the boy's joke?
qa.a: As unkind and unfair. She says it is her friend's family's belief and asks whether he would laugh at his own grandmother's fast.

grounding: A teenager hears a joke about her religion from a classmate and feels ashamed, and a friend and a teacher speak up and call the stereotype false.

passage: In the Bengaluru school corridor, Uday, fourteen, had mentioned his church youth group when a classmate called out, "Careful, Uday will convert you!" Two boys laughed, and someone added, "They only make friends to convert people." Uday stared at his shoes. He wanted to say something clever, but nothing came out, and hot shame crept up his neck. Dev, who sat beside him in maths, stepped in. "Uday lent me his notes. That's all he's done." The boys drifted away. That afternoon Rekha Ma'am, the English teacher, heard about it from Dev and stopped the class. "The idea that a whole group of people all act one way is false, and it hurts real classmates. Nobody here is being recruited by anyone. If you have a question about a belief, ask it politely." Uday looked up. Dev gave him a small nod.

qa.q: Who stepped in when the classmates laughed at Uday?
qa.a: Dev, who sat beside Uday in maths, stepped in and said that Uday had only lent him notes.

qa.q: What is Uday feeling as he stares at his shoes?
qa.a: Uday feels ashamed and silenced. He wants to answer, but nothing comes out.

qa.q: What turning point protected Uday in the afternoon?
qa.a: Dev told Rekha Ma'am, and she stopped the class and named the idea as false, so the whole class heard that nobody was being recruited.

qa.q: How does Dev seem to see Uday?
qa.a: As a classmate and individual who lent notes, not as a stereotype. Dev speaks for Uday first and then reports it to the teacher.

grounding: A teenager hears a rumour about his faith from classmates and feels ashamed, and a friend and a teacher speak up and name the stereotype as false.

passage: After news of a riot in a city far away, Farhana stopped waiting at the bus stop. Farhana, who shared her Eid sewaiyan with Rashmi every year, now answered messages with one word. In their small town near Nashik, Rashmi, fifteen, felt a cold knot in her stomach. Jatin from class whispered that Farhana's family had warned her to stay away. Rashmi did not want to believe it. On Saturday she carried a packet of pakoras to Farhana's house. Farhana's mother let her in, and Farhana stared at the floor. "Have I done something?" Rashmi asked. "No," Farhana said finally. "Ammi is scared people will blame us for what strangers did." Rashmi shook her head. "I don't blame you for anything you didn't do. You're my friend." They ate the pakoras on the roof. On Monday Farhana was at the bus stop.

qa.q: What did Rashmi bring to Farhana's house?
qa.a: Rashmi brought a packet of pakoras.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when Farhana stopped answering properly?
qa.a: Rashmi felt worried and hurt, with a cold knot in her stomach, but she did not want to believe the rumour.

qa.q: Which choice by Rashmi kept the friendship alive?
qa.a: Rashmi went to Farhana's house, asked honestly whether she had done something, and said she did not blame Farhana for what strangers did.

qa.q: Why had Farhana pulled away?
qa.a: Farhana's mother was scared that people would blame their family for what strangers did, so Farhana stayed away out of fear and shame.

grounding: A teenager finds a friend of another faith pulling away after a news event and keeps trust alive by staying in touch and asking honestly.

passage: Kwame, fifteen, noticed that Ines had started eating lunch in the library. She used to save him a seat in the canteen and swap almond biscuits for his mum's plantain chips. Now she only nodded. Ines's family went to the mosque on Fridays, and Kwame sang in his church choir, and until now it had never mattered. After a week, Kwame texted, "Did I do something?" Ines wrote back, "No. My grandmother says I should stay with my own community after what was said about us on the news." The next day he found her at the tram stop. "I saw the news too," he said. "I don't think you or your family did anything. I'd hate to be blamed for what a stranger did." Ines's shoulders dropped. "I didn't want to bring trouble." "You're not trouble. I miss the biscuits." She laughed, the first time in a week.

qa.q: Where did Kwame find Ines the next day?
qa.a: Kwame found Ines at the tram stop.

qa.q: How might Kwame have felt when Ines began eating lunch in the library?
qa.a: Kwame probably felt puzzled, worried and a bit hurt, which is why he texted to ask whether he had done something.

qa.q: Which choice by Kwame kept the friendship alive?
qa.a: Kwame asked honestly by text, then went to find Ines and said he did not blame her or her family for what a stranger did.

qa.q: Why did Ines pull away?
qa.a: Ines's grandmother told her to stay with her own community after what was said on the news, and Ines did not want to bring trouble to Kwame.

grounding: A teenager finds a friend of another faith pulling away after a family warning and keeps trust alive by asking honestly and refusing to blame the friend.

passage: Zubin, my classmate at college, asked if he could join our Ganesh aarti, and I was curious how it would go. He arrived on time, left his shoes at the door and stood at the back with his hands loosely together, watching. He asked my mother quietly whether it was fine to take a photo of the idol. She said there was no need, and he nodded. When the aarti ended he took the prasad in his right hand, said thank you and asked what the modak stood for. My mother explained. He listened, asked one more question and told us about the fire temple where his family goes for Navroz. I can't say what he felt inside, but he looked interested, not pretending. At the door he said, "Thank you for letting me see it." Shreya

qa.q: What did Zubin ask after the aarti ended?
qa.a: Zubin asked what the modak stood for.

qa.q: What does Zubin's behaviour suggest he feels, and how sure can Shreya be?
qa.a: He seems interested and respectful, but Shreya cannot be certain of his inner state. Shreya only reads it from how he asked and listened.

qa.q: Which choices by Zubin showed respectful curiosity?
qa.a: He arrived on time, left his shoes at the door, stood at the back, asked before taking a photo, thanked the family and asked questions without pretending belief.

qa.q: How might Shreya's mother have felt answering Zubin's questions?
qa.a: Probably welcoming and glad to explain, since she answered patiently and told him there was no need for a photo.

grounding: A young adult attends a friend's family prayer to learn, asking respectfully and following local etiquette without any wish to change belief.

passage: Saturday. Avni asked her friend Asif, "Could I come to your family's iftar next week and watch the evening prayer? I want to learn, not to join." Asif smiled. "Ask Ammi, she'll be happy. Bring a dupatta for your head and leave your shoes outside." Wednesday. At Asif's home the family laid out the prayer mats. Avni sat quietly on a chair by the wall, head covered, and took no photos. Afterwards she asked Asif's mother, "Would it be all right to ask what you say?" and listened carefully to the answer. She ate dates and did not pretend to pray. Friday. Avni texted Asif: "Thank you. I felt welcome. I'm still myself, but I understand a little more."

qa.q: On which day did Avni ask Asif about the iftar?
qa.a: Avni asked Asif on Saturday.

qa.q: How does Avni seem to feel by Friday?
qa.a: Avni feels welcome and grateful. Avni thanks Asif and says, "I'm still myself, but I understand a little more."

qa.q: Which choice by Avni at Asif's home showed respect without pretending?
qa.a: She sat quietly with her head covered, took no photos, asked politely what was said, and did not pretend to pray.

qa.q: How might Asif's mother have felt when Avni asked what she says?
qa.a: Probably pleased and respected, since Avni asked politely and listened carefully to the answer.

grounding: A young adult attends a friend's family prayer to learn, asking respectfully and following etiquette without any wish to change belief.

passage: Rajni, you asked why I keep a plate of sewaiyan aside for Farida's family on Eid, so listen. I am Lokesh, your Nana. When your mother was twenty, she came home glowing about her friend Farida, and I felt fear rising. What will the neighbours say? Will she forget our traditions? I nearly said, "Stop seeing her." Instead, one night at dinner I asked, "What do you like about Farida?" Your mother said, "She never laughs at anyone. When I lost my purse on the train, she gave me her own fare home." I went quiet. That was not a label. That was a person. I still worried, but I invited Farida's family for Diwali, and her mother brought sewaiyan a few months later. My fears lost their sharp edges slowly. Your mother and Farida still speak every Sunday.

qa.q: What did Lokesh ask at dinner instead of saying "Stop seeing her"?
qa.a: He asked, "What do you like about Farida?"

qa.q: What was Lokesh afraid of when Rajni's mother came home glowing about Farida?
qa.a: Lokesh was afraid of what the neighbours would say and that she might forget their traditions.

qa.q: What choice did Lokesh make instead of banning the friendship, and what did it lead to?
qa.a: He asked about Farida and listened, which led to hearing about her kindness and to inviting Farida's family for Diwali.

qa.q: How might Rajni's mother have felt when he asked what she liked about Farida?
qa.a: Probably relieved and heard. She answered warmly with a story about Farida's kindness instead of having to defend her.

grounding: A parent worries about a young adult child's close friend of another faith, and honest conversation about values, not labels, replaces a ban.

passage: Nilesh had learned from a neighbour that his son Bhupen, twenty, spent Eid at his friend Kabir's house. Now the two of them were stuck in the car on the flyover approach, the jam already twenty minutes old, and neither could leave. Nilesh gripped the wheel. "People are talking, Bhupen. They say you're at Kabir's house every week." Bhupen sighed. "Papa, ask me what you actually want to ask." Nilesh swallowed. "I'm afraid you'll drift from us. And I'm afraid of what people will say." "Kabir studied with me every night before my exams," Bhupen said quietly. "He never asked me to change anything, and I don't ask him." Nilesh watched the red brake lights ahead. "Invite Kabir for Diwali," he said finally. "I'd like to meet Kabir properly."

qa.q: Where were Nilesh and Bhupen when they had this talk?
qa.a: They were in the car in a traffic jam on the flyover approach.

qa.q: What is Nilesh afraid of when he grips the wheel?
qa.a: Nilesh is afraid that Bhupen will drift from the family and afraid of what people will say.

qa.q: What turning point led Nilesh to invite Kabir for Diwali?
qa.a: Bhupen answered honestly about what Kabir means to him, that Kabir studied with him and never asked him to change, and Nilesh then spoke about his real fear.

qa.q: How does Bhupen see his friendship with Kabir?
qa.a: As a loyal, mutual friendship based on help and respect: Kabir never asks Bhupen to change anything, and Bhupen does not ask Kabir.

grounding: A parent worries about a young adult child's close friend of another faith, and an honest talk about values leads to an invitation instead of a ban.

passage: Sunday night. Vidya and I finally sat down with a notebook and made three columns: names, rites, children. Names: we each keep our own. Rites: a short ceremony at the temple and a blessing at her church, so both families see themselves in it. Children: they will learn both our festivals and stories, and choose for themselves when they are older. We disagreed about who would speak to whose parents first; Vidya wanted me to speak to hers, and I said I would go with her to both. My mother thinks people will talk. Vidya's father worries about her faith being lost. I am afraid of both conversations, and glad we started before the wedding was booked. It's not that everything is decided. It's that neither of us had to win. Chaitanya

qa.q: What three columns did Vidya and Chaitanya make in the notebook?
qa.a: They made three columns: names, rites and children.

qa.q: How does Chaitanya feel about the two family conversations ahead?
qa.a: Chaitanya feels afraid of both conversations but glad that the couple started early, before the wedding was booked.

qa.q: Which choice by the couple made their planning work?
qa.a: They talked early and settled each point together: each keeps a name, both rites are honoured, and the children learn both traditions, so neither had to win.

qa.q: What might Vidya's father be worried about?
qa.a: He worries that Vidya's faith might be lost, which is a real fear behind his concern.

grounding: A couple from different faiths negotiates names, rites and their children's upbringing early and with mutual respect while both families worry.

passage: Avni: We talked about baby names last night. Danish wants an Urdu name, I want a Sanskrit one. We laughed, then went quiet. Jaya: How did you leave it? Avni: A name both families can say easily, plus a middle name from each side. Nobody wins, both belong. Jaya: And the rites? Avni: A registry signing first. Then a nikah at his home and a small puja at mine, same weekend. His mum asked if I will convert. I said no, kindly, and she said she just wanted to know. Jaya: Brave. And your parents? Avni: Papa is worried people will talk. I told him it's early, and we'll speak together next Sunday. Jaya: Proud of you 🙂

qa.q: Which names did Danish and Avni each want for a baby?
qa.a: Danish wants an Urdu name and Avni wants a Sanskrit one.

qa.q: How does Avni feel about telling Papa, and what shows it?
qa.a: Avni feels a little nervous but steady. Avni tells Papa it is early and plans to speak together the next Sunday.

qa.q: What choice did Avni make when Danish's mum asked about converting, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Avni answered no, kindly, and Danish's mum said she just wanted to know. It kept the talk honest and respectful without a fight.

qa.q: How might Danish's mum have felt when she asked that question?
qa.a: Probably curious and a little anxious, since she wanted to know where things stood and accepted the honest answer calmly.

grounding: A couple from different faiths negotiates names, rites and children's upbringing while both families worry, with clear early talks and mutual respect.

subtype: Standing beside a neighbour under threat [Response]
passage: The lights went out across the lane just as the shouting started outside Mr. Ansari's door. Naveen, twenty-five, saw torches and a knot of men in the dark, one of them yelling about what Mr. Ansari's family cooked. Naveen's heart pounded. He didn't shout back. He called down to his flatmate Sumit, "Get the other neighbours, quietly," and walked across in his slippers. "Uncle, I'm here," he said, standing beside the old man at the door. Mrs. Rao arrived with her torch, then two more families. The men saw a small crowd of neighbours and no fight. Naveen said calmly, "We know this house. Please go home." They muttered and left. Later Naveen rang the society secretary to report it, and the secretary promised to come in the morning with the guard and speak to everyone.

qa.q: Who did Naveen ask Sumit to get?
qa.a: Naveen asked Sumit to get the other neighbours, quietly.

qa.q: What does Naveen feel when he sees the torches and the men?
qa.a: Naveen is frightened, since his heart pounds, but he stays calm and does not shout back.

qa.q: Which choice by Naveen helped Mr. Ansari most?
qa.a: Naveen walked across and stood beside Mr. Ansari, called the neighbours to join, and spoke calmly instead of trading insults.

qa.q: How might Mr. Ansari have felt when the neighbours arrived?
qa.a: Probably relieved and less alone, since Naveen stood beside him and other families came to the door.

grounding: A young adult stands beside a neighbour of another faith facing hostility, brings other neighbours and reports it, without stoking anger at anyone.

subtype: Standing beside a neighbour under threat [Response]
passage: Vishal noticed the folded note taped to Seema's door on Monday morning: "Your kind not welcome here." Seema, a Christian neighbour on the third floor who taught music at home, was standing in the corridor holding it, her jaw tight. Vishal, twenty-four, did not say "how awful" and walk on. He said, "May I stand with you for a minute? Shall we take this to the society secretary together?" They went down. The secretary, Mr. Batra, read the note twice. "This is not acceptable. I will put up a notice and ask the guard to keep watch after ten." Seema thanked him quietly. That evening Vishal knocked with a plate of pohe and asked if he could sit in on her Saturday music class; he had always wanted to learn the keys. She smiled for the first time that day.

qa.q: What did the note taped to Seema's door say?
qa.a: The note said, "Your kind not welcome here."

qa.q: What might Vishal be feeling as he asks if he may stand with her?
qa.a: Vishal is concerned and careful, wanting to help without taking over or making it worse.

qa.q: Which choice by Vishal helped Seema most on Monday?
qa.a: Vishal stayed with her and went with her to the society secretary, so the note was reported together and Mr. Batra promised a notice and a watch.

qa.q: What might Seema be feeling when she holds the note, and later when she smiles?
qa.a: At first Seema is hurt and shaken, with a tight jaw. Later she feels some comfort, since a neighbour offered company and the secretary took it seriously.

grounding: A young adult offers company and a voice when a neighbour of another faith is targeted with hostility, and goes with her to the society secretary.

passage: I was nine when I asked if God is real. At home, Nani said, "Of course, God sees everything, beta." Next morning at school I asked Sarika Ma'am. She did not say yes or no. She said, "People believe different things. Some believe in God, some don't, and many are still wondering. What do you think?" I said I didn't know. She said that was an honest answer. That night I told Nani, "Ma'am says people believe different things." Nani was quiet, then said, "That is true too. In our family we pray." I thought about it for days. It was strange to have two answers, but nobody was angry. I still ask questions, and no one tells me I'm wrong for asking. Parveen

qa.q: What did Sarika Ma'am say when Parveen asked if God is real?
qa.a: Sarika Ma'am said that people believe different things, that some believe in God, some don't, and many are still wondering, and asked what Parveen thought.

qa.q: How did Parveen feel about getting two different answers?
qa.a: Parveen felt curious and calm. It was strange to have two answers, but nobody was angry, so Parveen kept thinking about it.

qa.q: Which choice by Nani kept trust between her and Parveen?
qa.a: Nani stayed quiet, then said that what Ma'am said is true too and that in their family they pray, instead of arguing.

qa.q: How might Nani have felt when Parveen repeated what Ma'am said?
qa.a: Probably thoughtful and a little surprised, since she went quiet first, but she was willing to accept it.

grounding: A child asks whether God is real and gets different answers at home and at school, and calm honest replies that people believe differently keep curiosity and trust.

passage: Note to Jaya's parents, Class 5. During circle time today, Jaya, eight, asked, "Does God really exist? My Nani says yes, but my friend's father says no." The class went quiet. I said, "People believe different things, and that is allowed. Some people pray, some don't. What do you think, Jaya?" Jaya said, "I think maybe yes, but I want to find out." I told her that asking is good, and that she can talk with her family about what they believe. Two other children shared what their families believe, and nobody laughed. Jaya seemed relaxed afterwards. I would gently encourage you to keep answering her questions calmly. Vasudha, class teacher

qa.q: What did Jaya ask during circle time?
qa.a: Jaya asked, "Does God really exist?" and said Nani says yes but a friend's father says no.

qa.q: What might Jaya be feeling when she says "I think maybe yes, but I want to find out"?
qa.a: Jaya is curious and thoughtful, and feels safe enough to say she is unsure and wants to explore.

qa.q: Which choice by Vasudha kept the class calm and curious?
qa.a: Vasudha said that people believe different things and that this is allowed, and asked Jaya what she thinks instead of giving one answer.

qa.q: How might the two other children have felt when they shared their family beliefs?
qa.a: Probably safe and included, since nobody laughed and the teacher said that different beliefs are allowed.

grounding: A child asks whether God is real and the teacher answers calmly that people believe differently, protecting the child's curiosity and trust.
